Article Title: Rohit Sharma to coach Mumbai Indians? Ashwin makes bold prediction
Article Text:
Mumbai Indians' Rohit Sharma (PTI Photo)

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Former India spinner Ravichandran Ashwin believes Rohit Sharma could have a significant role to play in coaching or mentoring after his playing career comes to an end, with the former India spinner urging Mumbai Indians to bring their long-time captain into the franchise setup as soon as he decides to retire.Indian men’s cricket has gone through a relatively quiet phase over the past month following the Lord’s ODI against England, with IPL trade discussions and changes in international coaching setups dominating the conversation.Against that backdrop, Ashwin was asked about the possibility of India’s two modern batting greats, Rohit Sharma and Virat Kohli , eventually moving into coaching.While Ashwin could see Rohit taking up a role with Mumbai Indians, he was less certain about Kohli making an immediate transition into coaching. The former spinner suggested Kohli may instead prefer to step away from the game for some time.“I don’t think Virat will be ready to become a coach immediately," Ashwin said on his YouTube channel. “I think both have worked a lot. Maybe Rohit Sharma could come into the Mumbai Indians in some capacity. I don’t know about Virat, honestly—Virat will probably want to take a break, in my opinion."Ashwin also believes the growing importance of franchise cricket could create more specialist positions for former players.He expects roles such as mentor, director of cricket and high-performance director to become increasingly common, giving successful cricketers multiple avenues to remain involved with the sport after retirement.Rohit, 39, is already approaching the final stage of his playing career. He has retired from both T20Is and Tests, while his future in the remaining format continues to attract attention.For Ashwin, however, Rohit’s tactical understanding makes him too valuable for Mumbai Indians to simply lose once he stops playing. The veteran batter led the franchise to five IPL titles and was also part of India’s successful run to an ICC World Cup triumph.“If tomorrow Rohit decides ‘I won’t play,’ Mumbai Indians should immediately absorb him," Ashwin said. “A captain who won five titles and led India to a World Cup—you won’t find such people. If he doesn’t want to be head coach because it’s a labor-intensive role, but after a one-two year break, he’ll be ready to take up a role. Like Rahul bhai took a break and then came back to work. So I think they should immediately absorb such cricketers and not let them go. And knowing the Mumbai Indians, they won’t let go of a player with Rohit Sharma’s thinking capacity," he added.Ashwin’s comments suggest he sees Rohit’s future involvement in cricket extending beyond the traditional head coach role. A period away from the game could allow the former India captain to recharge before potentially returning in a strategic or mentoring position.Kohli, meanwhile, could follow a different path, with Ashwin expecting the former India captain to take time away from cricket before deciding what comes next.With franchise cricket continuing to expand its influence, Ashwin believes retired stars such as Rohit and Kohli could have opportunities in several areas beyond conventional coaching, provided they are given the freedom to choose the roles that suit them best.
Article Summary: Former India spinner Ravichandran Ashwin believes Rohit Sharma could have a significant role to play in coaching or mentoring after his playing career. Ashwin urges Mumbai Indians to bring their long-time captain into the franchise setup as soon as he decides to retire. The 39-year-old could see Rohit taking up a role with Mumbai Indians.

Article Title: 'I'd love players to be mobbed like IPL cricketers': The push to make esports mainstream
Article Text:
Mike McCabe

Chess in Esports : The odd game out

Paris was never the plan

An IPL-sized ambition

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

There is a chessboard on the big screens at the Esports World Cup 2026 in Paris Expo Porte de Versailles, surrounded by the production, noise, and visual language of an event built around competitive gaming. For Mike McCabe, that is not an oddity. It is a glimpse of where esports is heading.Chess was added to the Esports World Cup in 2025 and is back in Paris this year, with the 2026 tournament carrying USD 1.5 million prize money. The field includes players such as Magnus Carlsen, Alireza Firouzja and India's four Grandmasters - Arjun Erigaisi (Gen.G Esports), Nihal Sarin, Aravindh Chithambaram, Pranesh M (all S8UL Esports)The game is also the obvious outlier in the EWC programme. It has been played competitively for centuries. Its rules did not emerge from a game publisher. Its stars did not grow up inside the esports industry.And yet, sitting alongside the other titles in Paris, McCabe believes chess fits. “For us, what qualifies as an esport really comes down to the community and the ecosystem,” McCabe, COO and Deputy CEO of the Esports Foundation, told The Times of India in Paris on the sidelines of the Esports World Cup 2026.“And so when we look at any game that people are playing digitally, if there's a really strong competitive ecosystem, there's organised events, there's rankings, there's an understanding and there's an interest from people to watch and spectate, then it can live within the world of esports.”McCabe isn't suggesting that chess has somehow crossed over and become a video game. That isn't really the point. What has changed is the way the EWC is looking at the game.For him, the question isn't whether chess looks like Rocket League or League of Legends. It is whether people play it competitively, whether there is an organised circuit around it, whether rankings and rivalries matter, and, crucially, whether people want to watch.That puts chess in an interesting place in Paris. It doesn't have to shed its history to sit alongside the newer games. It can arrive with all of it - the centuries of tradition, the familiar board, the Grandmasters - and still be part of this very modern, very loud version of competitive sport.And perhaps that is what makes chess more interesting to the EWC than simply being another title on the schedule. It tests how far the definition of esports can stretch without losing what makes the game itself recognisable.“What's unique about chess versus all the other esports, the other 23 games that we include in the tournament, is that it has a heritage that goes way beyond any of us and any of the world of traditional digital interactive entertainment,” McCabe said.“So it really is unique in that way. The rules have been there for generations.”“And what I love about it is it's the esport that we have here as part of the tournament that has that bridge between generations. I see lots of parents here with their kids. They've taught their kids to play this game.”That, for McCabe, is not just a nice feature of having chess at the EWC. It is part of the reason he thinks it works.“They didn't teach them how to play Rocket League or they didn't teach them how to play League of Legends, but they taught them how to play chess,” he said. “And they're able to enjoy this together.”“And I think it's a magical moment.”There is some evidence in his own experience of the tournament that the chess audience is behaving differently from what he has seen around some of the other games.“I know from many of my friends who've had more people hit me up this week for tickets than any other week of the seven weeks we've had,” McCabe said.That is the part of the chess story that is easy to miss if it is viewed simply as another title added to an esports schedule.The EWC is using chess to reach beyond the audience that already knows its games. Chess, in turn, gets a very different setting in which to present its best players.McCabe has India on his mind when he talks about what the EWC could look like several years from now.But first comes a larger point. The definition of the games inside the EWC, he says, is not going to remain fixed.“I think we've always thought about it from the ecosystem, the audience and the viewership and the spectacle,” McCabe said.“The game definition is going to be something that's going to constantly evolve over time.”The EWC has been built around scale. This year's event has 24 games and a record USD 75 million prize pool across the competition.The move to Paris was not how the 2026 EWC was supposed to happen. Riyadh was meant to host it again before security concerns around the conflict in the region forced a change of plan.The Foundation quickly reframed Paris as the first international chapter of the EWC - and, now that the tournament is here, McCabe sees the move as evidence that the event was capable of doing what its organisers had always said it could.But the more interesting part of McCabe's answer is what he thinks happens after that. He is leaving the definition of the EWC - and perhaps esports itself - deliberately open, to the point where he is already looking five years ahead and wondering what games, formats and competitions might sit here that don't exist today.“And I'm excited what in five years time we're sitting down here and we're talking about what we've included. What is the latest innovation? What is the new competitive landscape that people are competing against?” he said.“Because that human passion is competing against each other. We've always done it ever since we first got onto this planet.”“And so that's something that I think is unique. And we're not constrained in the way that the traditional sport may be constrained.”“This is going to be a constantly new field of play that we explore.”Chess, then, is not necessarily the end point of that thinking. It is the current example.It also helps explain why McCabe is less concerned about whether a game looks like traditional esports and more interested in whether people care enough to compete, watch and follow its players.That becomes particularly interesting when he talks about what he wants the EWC to achieve in India. Asked what he would like to have proved wrong five years from now, McCabe does not start with the size of the prize pool or the number of games.“I'd love that players were walking along the streets in Chennai and being mobbed in the same way as an IPL cricketer is being mobbed,” he said.“That idea of people are recognized for their incredible abilities and they have the fandom, that would be one thing for me.”It is a very specific comparison. The IPL has spent years turning cricketers into recognisable sporting personalities, with franchises, rivalries, broadcasts and fan bases extending beyond the sport's traditional audience. McCabe wants esports players to reach a similar level of recognition.That ambition is also part of the reason the EWC has expanded beyond individual games into clubs, teams and a wider competition between organisations. But Paris has given McCabe another reason to believe the model can travel.The move from Riyadh was completed in a remarkably short period. The EWC may describe Paris as its first international chapter, while McCabe sees the relocation as evidence that the property can operate beyond its home market.“Esports has always been mobile,” he said. “It's always been an event that has taken place in different parts of the world, different world tournaments, whether it be League of Legends Worlds or Call of Duty, majors have happened all around the planet.”The difference, he argues, was the speed. “What's different is the pace with which this was done. Those events normally take many months to prepare and to be able to build the groundwork.”The EWC had to move a global event to another country, build it and operate it in a short period.“This is like moving, well it is, it's a global sporting event to a completely different country designing, building and operating in an incredibly short time frame,” McCabe said.“And what it's shown is how partnership between a government, between the publishers, the clubs and ourselves has been able to make, honestly, a miracle happen.”For McCabe, Paris therefore answers two different questions. Chess has shown that the EWC does not necessarily have to restrict itself to the conventional boundaries of esports.Paris has shown that the EWC itself does not necessarily have to remain in one place. The harder question is whether both ideas can be sustained.McCabe knows the EWC has been built aggressively, with investment helping it reach a scale that traditional sports properties took decades to achieve.“So if you think about traditional sport that takes decades, if not longer, to build to a global scale, we just wanted to shortcut that,” he said. “And so we've accelerated massively.”The commercial test now becomes more important. McCabe points to the arrival of major brands such as Allianz, Hilton Hotels and Sony, alongside the traditional technology and gaming companies that have historically supported esports.“What we're seeing is now a move from brands that are associated with esports, whether they be technology partners or peripherals or others, to actually having blue-chip partners involved.”The next piece, he says, is media rights. “And that's something that we will need to change and evolve that gives funding to the clubs. It gives funding to the partners, the publishers, and also helps us to build that long-term sustainability.”There is a lot still to be proved. But chess has already given McCabe something that the EWC's more conventional games cannot. A connection to people who may not think of themselves as esports fans.Parents bringing children to watch a game they already know. Grandmasters representing esports organisations. Traditional chess audiences watching their players in an environment built around gaming. And a new generation of players being introduced to the game through a tournament that would otherwise have nothing to do with their usual sporting calendar.McCabe sees that as the beginning rather than the conclusion. The EWC will return to Riyadh next year. It may eventually move again. The list of games may change. The definition of what belongs in the competition may change with it.But when McCabe looks five years ahead, the thing he wants to see is not another statistic.“I would love to be operating in bigger and bigger venues,” he said. “For us, it's reaching more and more people and we're incredibly privileged to be able to have this opportunity to put on this amazing event.”“And I just want to be able to connect with more people over the years to come,” he added.
Article Summary: Chess was added to the EWC in 2025 and is back in Paris this year. The 2026 tournament carries USD 1.5 million prize money. The field includes players such as Magnus Carlsen, Alireza Firouzja and India's four Grandmasters.

Article Title: IND vs SL 1st Test: India may unleash three left-arm spinners in Galle as Morkel drops big hint
Article Text:
Ravindra Jadeja, front left, and Manav Suthar, front right, during a practice session. (PTI Photo)

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

India could field three left-arm spinners, with Ravindra Jadeja Kuldeep Yadav and Manav Suthar all in contention for the first Test against Sri Lanka in Galle.As expected, the Galle International Stadium pitch underwent a ‘haircut’ on Wednesday, three days before the Test. With the surface expected to favour spin as the match progresses, India’s bowling coach Morne Morkel dropped a strong hint that the three left-armers could be India’s preferred spin combination.“Kuldeep is there and he’s an attacking sort of bowler. For us, his experience and class can’t be overlooked. They’re all different in their own way — one (Suthar) turns it a bit more, one (Jadeja) is slightly more accurate. I don’t think three left-arm spinners are a massive concern for us. It’s about how (captain Shubman) Gill uses them at certain times. In terms of skill, they have what it takes to get 20 wickets for us,” Morkel told reporters in Galle on Thursday.Jadeja is an automatic pick, while Suthar impressed in the recent tour game in Sri Lanka. Kuldeep, meanwhile, is a left-arm wrist-spinner.The pitch had a brownish look two days before the Test and is expected to offer good batting conditions initially before turning increasingly.“For sure, it’s a good-looking surface. I’d be slightly surprised if it goes the other way. Traditionally, at this venue, the first two days belong to the batting side, or your first innings.So that will be important to whatever happens at the toss. If you bat first, make sure you go big; if you bowl first, get the ball in the right areas,” Morkel said.India could also opt for three pacers — Mohammed Siraj , Prasidh Krishna and Gurnoor Brar, who took 10 wickets for India ‘A’ during their shadow tour of Sri Lanka last month and is in line for his Test debut.Morkel said the heat, humidity and the Kookaburra ball going soft early would test India’s quicks. He urged them to bowl short, high-intensity spells and make the most of the conditions. “It’s about the mindset. As a fast bowler, if you’re going to bowl short spells, put energy into the ball and hit good areas, you’ll always have an opportunity,” he said.Morkel also stressed the need for India’s quicks to be “street-smart” once the ball loses its hardness.
Article Summary: India could field three left-arm spinners against Sri Lanka. Ravindra Jadeja, Kuldeep Yadav and Manav Suthar all in contention. The Galle International Stadium pitch underwent a ‘haircut’ on Wednesday.

Article Title: Afghanistan Cricket Board wants India T20I shifted to festival date
Article Text:
Representative Image: Afghanistan cricketers (AP Photo)

MUMBAI: The Afghanistan Cricket Board (ACB) has approached the BCCI with a request to move one of the three T20Is against India in Sept to Sept 14, coinciding with Ganesh Chaturthi , TOI has learnt.The series is currently scheduled to be played in New Delhi on Sept 13, 15 and 17. Sources familiar with the developments said the ACB has asked if either the first or second game could be moved to Sept 14 as “a special gesture” and to add a festive touch to the growing cricketing ties between the two countries.“As a part of a special gesture, the ACB is considering Sept 14 as one of the match dates for the India-Afghanistan T20I series, coinciding with Ganesh Chaturthi, one of India’s most widely observed and auspicious festivals. If confirmed, the fixture could add a distinctive cultural dimension to the series and create a special occasion for cricket fans around the country,” ITW Universe, which is handling the series’ media rights, on-ground branding and production, said in a release.All three matches, which are to be hosted by the ACB, will be played in New Delhi.
Article Summary: Afghanistan Cricket Board (ACB) has approached the BCCI with a request to move one of the three T20Is against India in Sept to Sept 14, coinciding with Ganesh Chaturthi. The series is currently scheduled to be played in New Delhi on Sept 13, 15 and 17.

Article Title: ‘Be yourself, trust yourself’: The mental mantra driving India’s women hockey team
Article Text:
Indian women’s hockey team

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

As the Indian women’s hockey team puts the finishing touches to their preparations ahead of the World Cup, one individual has been making a difference off the field.Ben Wienk describes himself as a ‘Human Sports Innovator,’ and is helping the players understand themselves better and, in the process, discover their “unseen potential” — qualities that can ultimately help them perform better.“The goal is not for me to understand the player completely. I want her to understand herself better. What gives me energy? What matters to me? When do I feel confident? How do I learn best? What are my natural strengths? And what happens to me when the pressure increases?” Wienk, mental conditioning coach in the women’s hockey set-up, told TOI.And to do all this, he uses methods such as “profiling, personal conversations, observations and, above all, real-life situations”.It is not only about helping the players understand themselves better. Wienk’s work also gives head coach Sjoerd Marijne a better understanding of how to deal with each player.“Maybe if I shout at one player, she freezes and it doesn’t work. I may have to be more friendly with her. With another player, maybe I have to shout because that works for her,” Marijne said.Wienk further explained saying, “A coaching message can work immediately for one player while creating uncertainty in another.One player needs short, concrete information, while another first wants to understand the bigger picture.”Therein lies the importance of his role. In a team where players come from different backgrounds and with different personalities, there is no one-size-fits-all approach. The idea is not to make everyone think or respond in the same way. It is to understand what makes each player tick and find the best way to bring out her strengths.It’s challenging, but that is precisely what attracted Wienk to the assignment in the first place.“This assignment brings so many different elements together: elite sport, different personalities and backgrounds, a fascinating culture, and at the same time the ambition to perform at the very highest international level,” said the Dutchman.And when he first started working with the team, he was impressed by what he saw.“The first thing that struck me was the enormous drive and willingness to work hard. There is a great deal of ambition within this group,” he said.That ambition has taken the team forward this year. India qualified for the World Cup, showed encouraging signs in Argentina and Australia and then went on to win the Nations Cup. But the World Cup is a different ball game, and that’s where Wienk’s work could be put to its biggest test.Wienk is not trying to remove pressure from the players. Instead, he wants them to understand what happens to them when the pressure increases. “The goal is not for a player to suddenly become someone else under pressure. The goal is for her to know herself well enough to stay close to her own strengths under pressure while continuing to trust her teammates,” he said.And the players, too, appear to be enjoying the process.“We worked on trusting and communicating with each other and building a connection within the team. I particularly enjoyed the blindfold exercise, where we had to guide each other. It showed us how important it is to trust our teammates and react quickly to their calls,” said Shilpi Dabas, one of the newcomers in the team.The real test, however, will come when India walk out for their World Cup opener against China on Sunday. Wienk has a simple message for them.“Be yourself. Trust yourself. Trust each other. And do it together.”The World Cup is only the first of two major challenges, with the Asian Games to follow soon after. For Wienk, the way to deal with that pressure is equally simple: “Keep the ambition big, but the daily task small.”For now, the task is the World Cup. And for India, the hope is that understanding themselves — and each other — a little better will help them make the most of what they already have.
Article Summary: Ben Wienk is a mental conditioning coach in the Indian women's hockey team. He is helping the players understand themselves better and discover their ‘unseen potential’ He uses methods such as ‘profiling, personal conversations, observations and, above all, real-life situations’

Article Title: BWF World Championships: For Satwiksairaj Rankireddy, Chirag Shetty’s pain is his own as the pair eyes gold
Article Text:
Chirag Shetty and Satwiksairaj Rankireddy

Satwik's new smash trick: Less shoulder, more wrist

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: For Satwiksairaj Rankireddy , injury is never a one-man problem. When his shoulder hurts, somewhere along the way, Chirag Shetty hurts too.That is the peculiar reality of a partnership that has grown far beyond the boundaries of a badminton court. The two are among India's most successful men's doubles combinations, but Satwik's recent injury layoff has also brought home just how deeply their fortunes are intertwined."It’s more tough mentally than physically to prepare,” Satwik told TOI in an interview ahead of the World Championships, beginning Aug 17. “It’s always difficult handling things which are not in your control. That was the toughest part. Few things you can’t handle. So, I think that was very frustrating and you are disturbing the other person’s life as well.”He paused to put the relationship in perspective.“When we both are healthy, both are playing good, it’s good for both. Otherwise, it’s really frustrating for the other partner.”The timing could hardly have been more cruel. After a promising start to 2026, Satwik and Chirag reached the Thailand Open final before ending a 742-day wait for a World Tour title by winning the Singapore Open.They beat world No. 1 Kim Won Ho and Seo Seung-jae in the Singapore semifinals before overcoming Fajar Alfian and Muhammad Shohibul Fikri in the final.Then came the roadblock. Satwik's recurring shoulder problem forced the pair out of the Indonesia Open and later the Japan Open, disrupting the rhythm they had painstakingly rebuilt.“I think it was difficult, but it’s part and parcel of sport. It’s how you overcome it and come back stronger,” Chirag said. “We are more than ready to do our best at the Worlds."The comeback has been deliberately cautious. Satwik and Chirag have now trained together at the Gopichand badminton academy in Hyderabad for more than a month, although Satwik initially avoided his full smash. The priority was simple: “being 100 percent injury-free and pain-free,” Chirag said.Now comes the biggest test — a home Worlds event after 17 years, where the fifth-seed, World No. 5 Indians have a first-round bye and begin in the Round of 32 against Indonesia's Ryan Indra and Nikolais Joaquin.The field is unforgiving: Korean leaders Kim Won Ho-Seo Seung-jae, Malaysia’s Aaron Chia-Soh Wooi Yik, China’s Liang Weikeng-Wang Chang and He Jiting-Ren Xiangyu, Indonesia’s Fajar-Fikri and Sabar Karyaman Gutama-Muhammad Reza Pahlevi Isfahani, Malaysia’s Goh Sze Fei-Nur Izzuddin and Japan’s Takuro Hoki-Yugo Kobayashi are among the threats.Yet Satwik refuses to look beyond the next match. “We are just focusing on ourselves,” he said. “It’s always better to take one match at a time. Not to think way, way ahead.”They already own Worlds bronze medals from 2022 and 2025. A third podium finish would further cement their place among India's badminton greats. But this time, on home soil, the ambition is bigger: to change the colour of the medal in front of a home crowd.“We can’t keep these things away...pressure of expectations would be there,” Chirag said. “But we are taking it in a positive way. People are here to support us.”And so, amid the noise, Satwik has reduced the mission to its simplest form: “My job is to focus on my rehab. Practice. Warm up. Stretching. Eat well. Sleep well. Play well. That’s it.”After the Worlds, the pair will keep their Asian Games workload selective, with Chirag confirming that the China Open will be their only tournament before the continental showpiece.Satwik’s trademark power game is getting a small but significant tweak as he returns from his shoulder injury.“I use my whole shoulder when I’m hitting the smash. Few people use only forearm and wrist and all these things. But I use my whole shoulder. So that’s why I get all the time some issues with my shoulder.”The solution is not to abandon the attacking game that has made Satwik-Chirag one of the most feared pairs in badminton, but to distribute the load better.“I have started using my wrist and forearm as well,” he said. "I'm using my shoulder and wrist and forearm. Instead of using that full shoulder, I started using other muscles as well.”For Satwik, it is a subtle adjustment aimed at making his biggest weapon more sustainable. "I’m not using the whole shoulder like I do all the time...kind of using more of the forearm and wrist.”
Article Summary: Satwiksairaj Rankireddy and Chirag Shetty are among India's most successful men's doubles combinations. Satwik's recurring shoulder problem forced the pair out of the Indonesia Open and later the Japan Open. The pair have now trained together at the Gopichand badminton academy in Hyderabad.

Article Title: Tilottama Sen resets her targets after teen ‘angst’, makes Asian Games team
Article Text:
Tilottama Sen

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

PUNE: The pain of winning a quota place and not being able to represent the country can hurt. It took Tilottama Sen months to get out of disappointment.Today, more than two years after the heartbreak — and a year after she returned to shooting — Tilottama has made it to the Asian Games team.The shooter had become the youngest to win an Olympic quota when she booked a berth in women’s 10m air rifle ahead of the Paris Olympics over two years ago. However, the teenager couldn’t represent India as she lost her place to Ramita in the trials. The setback was difficult to process for the shooter, only 15 then.She was angry, not at herself, nor the federation, but chose to take it out at her event — 10m air rifle.“I was very angry at it; I started hating the event (10m). I quit shooting for some months and didn’t feel like getting back to the range,” Tilottama, now 17, told TOI.With the support of her parents, the youngster was then introduced to a new friend — 50m rifle 3-position event. “I met Manoj sir (coach Manoj Kumar) who asked me to try 3 positions. I was sure I didn’t want to start shooting again if it was 10m, so I gave 3P a try,” she said.While she said she had moved on, it wasn’t easy for her. “I was frustrated and disillusioned when it happened. It was not easy to get out of it. My parents supported me; my psychologist helped me.She asked me to read and paint to get over the disappointment. I focused on my studies. It took time, but I managed to walk out of it. I am at peace with it now,” the Bengaluru-based shooter said.She agreed to a new discipline, but it wasn’t easy. “I started training for one position at a time. I first trained for kneeling, then switched to prone and shifted to standing position last. It was tedious, but I had to take it slow and learn the basics first before I started training for competitions,” she said.After she started training for 3P, Tilottama ‘forgave’ her first event. “I am not angry at it anymore. I now train for both the events,” she said.“I am happy that I have qualified to participate in my first multisport event. I will try to focus on the present and the future now,” she said.
Article Summary: Tilottama Sen was the youngest to win an Olympic quota when she booked a berth in women’s 10m air rifle ahead of the Paris Olympics over two years ago. The setback was difficult to process for the shooter, only 15 then. “I was very angry at it; I started hating the event (10m) I quit shooting for some months and didn’t feel like getting back to the range,” she said.

Article Title: India's 11 World Cup debutants: Deepika, Shilpi's remarkable journeys to Hockey's biggest stage
Article Text:
Photo caption: Deepika Soreng (left) and Shilpi Dabas with her parents (Credit: TOI)

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

WC debutants:

When the Indian women’s team opens its World Cup campaign against China on Sunday, 11 players in the squad will be making their World Cup debuts. They come from different corners of the country — Mizoram, Jharkhand, Odisha, Haryana, Maharashtra, Madhya Pradesh and Punjab — and have taken different paths to reach hockey’s biggest stage.Some grew up with the sport, others took it up after playing different sports, while for some, hockey became a route to a better life. One of them is Jharkhand’s Deepika Soreng, who grew up in Simdega district and was introduced to hockey by Father Benedict Kujur at RC Upgraded Middle School in Karangaguri, where students were required to bring a hockey stick to school.Life, however, was far from certain. Deepika’s father died when she was a child, leaving her mother, Friska, to take up whatever work she could to support her daughter and two sons.“When I later got a chance to join the residential academy in Simdega, my mother went to Rourkela to work at the steel plant,” said Deepika, one of three students of late coach Pratima Barwa — alongside Salima Tete and Beauty Dungdung — who will play at the World Cup.Friska spent more than a decade working at the steel plant, living away from her children so they could continue their education and pursue their dreams. Years later, after Deepika broke into the national team and secured a job with the Railways, she was finally able to bring her mother back home.Friska now lives in Ranchi in her daughter’s apartment. “Next, I would like to take my mother somewhere by air. She has never travelled by flight, and I really want her to experience that at least once,” Deepika said.Because of the circumstances, Friska has not been able to follow her daughter’s hockey journey closely. She knows Deepika plays hockey and represents India, but herself knows little about the game itself. In another corner of the country, Anita Dabas, however, has closely followed her daughter Shilpi’s every step as she tried to break into the national team. A former national player from Haryana who also represented Air India, Anita made it to the India camp around 30 years ago.“She couldn’t make the team eventually. But now Shilpi has got that opportunity to represent India at the World Cup and it feels like the dream of the entire family has come true,” Shilpi’s father Anil, told TOI from their home in Sonipat. For Shilpi, the wait has been agonising. She has been playing senior nationals since 2018, but it was only earlier this year that she finally received a call-up to the senior national camp following her performance in Women’s Hockey India League with SG Pipers.“I had been trying for many years. Whenever there was a national selection or tournament, I would think, ‘Maybe my name will come this time.’ I would feel that surely it would happen now, but it just wasn’t happening,” the 28-year-old told TOI from Netherlands. There were moments of frustration, but Shilpi never stopped working. Her parents and coach Pritam Siwach ensured she kept going through the difficult years.“She would get irritated and frustrated at times. There were many occasions when I had to motivate her,” said Pritam.The persistence has now paid off. Shilpi has not only sealed her place in the World Cup squad but also played a major role in India’s Nations Cup triumph in June. Anil credits the Haryana state association and her first coach, Rajinder Singh Sr., a member of India’s 1980 Moscow Olympics gold medal-winning squad, for playing important roles in her development. Pratima did much the same for Deepika, guiding her for almost a decade before her death last year. Deepika, however, will carry her coach’s memory when she takes the field on Sunday, as will Salima and Beauty.And while they will share the same World Cup stage, the journeys that brought Deepika and Shilpi there could hardly have been more different. They were on two very different paths leading to the same dream.Lalthantluangi, Shilpi Dabas, Ishika Chaudhary, Sakshi Rana, Sunelita Toppo, Deepika Soreng, DeepikaRutuja Dadaso Pisal, Ishika, Baljeet Kaur, Beauty Dungdung
Article Summary: 11 players in the squad will be making their World Cup debuts. They come from different corners of the country. Some grew up with the sport, others took it up after playing different sports. For some, hockey became a route to a better life. Deepika Soreng's father died when she was a child.

Article Title: Subroto Cup to kick off on August 18; 107 teams to compete across three age categories

Air Marshal S. Sivakumar during the official announcement event for 65th Subroto Cup. (PTI Photo)

NEW DELHI: The 65th edition of the prestigious Subroto Cup International Football Tournament will kick off on August 18, with 107 teams set to compete across three age categories in New Delhi NCR and Bengaluru.The tournament, organised by the Subroto Mukerjee Sports Education Society (SMSES) under the aegis of the Air Force Sports Control Board, will be held until Sept 24. The competition will feature Junior Girls (U-17), Sub-Junior Boys (U-15) and Junior Boys (U-17), with more than 215 matches scheduled across the three categories.The official announcement was made on Wednesday in the presence of Air Marshal S. Sivakumar VSM, Air Officer-in-Charge Administration and Vice Chairman of SMSES, who attended as the chief guest. Former India footballer Ashalata Devi Loitongbam was also present as the guest of honour.“The Indian Air Force and SMSES are committed to making the tournament bigger and better every year, providing a platform for young athletes to take the next step in their careers,” Sivakumar said.The Junior Girls (U-17) competition will open the tournament in New Delhi, NCR, from Aug 18 to 27. The Sub-Junior Boys (U-15) category will be held in Bengaluru from Sept 1 to 9, before the Junior Boys (U-17) competition concludes the tournament in New Delhi NCR from Sept 15 to 24.Teams representing various states, Union Territories and educational bodies will participate, with Sri Lanka providing international representation. An age-determination test will also be conducted for the Sub-Junior Boys category in Bengaluru to ensure a level playing field.The matches will be played at venues including Ambedkar Stadium, Tejas Football Ground, Subroto Park Football Ground, Pinto Park Football Ground and Rajokri Football Ground in the Delhi-NCR region. In Bengaluru, Air Force School Jalahalli, Air Force School Yelahanka and Subroto Football Ground Jalahalli will host matches.Farook Higher Secondary School of Kerala is the defending champion in the Junior Boys' category, while Betkuchi High School of Guwahati (Assam) holds the Junior Girls' title. Minerva Public School (CISCE) is the reigning Sub-Junior Boys champion.First held in 1960, the Subroto Cup was conceived by Air Marshal Subroto Mukerjee to promote grassroots football across India.
Article Summary: The 65th edition of the prestigious Subroto Cup International Football Tournament will kick off on August 18. 107 teams will compete across three age categories in New Delhi NCR and Bengaluru. Former India footballer Ashalata Devi Loitongbam was the guest of honour at the official announcement event.

Article Title: Kuldeep, Jadeja, Suthar: Will India play three left-arm spinners in Galle? Coach drops hint

Kuldeep Yadav, Manav Suthar and Ravindra Jadeja

India could field three left-arm spinners in the first Test against Sri Lanka in Galle, with bowling coach Morne Morkel saying Kuldeep Yadav Ravindra Jadeja and Manav Suthar offer different skills and can form an attacking bowling combination.Kuldeep brings left-arm wrist spin and an attacking option, Jadeja relies on accuracy, while Suthar bowls a more traditional left-arm spin.“Kuldeep is there, and he's the attacking sort of bowler and for us, his experience and class can't look past. So yeah, I think for us they're all different in their way,” Morkel told the media here on Thursday.“So one (Suthar) turns a bit more, one (Jadeja) is slightly more accurate and I don't think it's a (three left-arm spinners) massive concern for us.“It’s just how Gill is going to use those guys at certain times. But yeah, I mean in terms of skill they've got the skill to get the 20 wickets for us,” he added.Morkel said the Galle pitch could also support the decision to play three spinners, with conditions expected to become more helpful to spin as the Test progresses.“Traditionally also if you look at the venue how it stacks and how it's been played up, that's sort of the way (three spinners) to go I think.The way we go with our spin bowling attack or spinners, it’s a very attacking option.“But looking at the surface, you know, to me, looks like a good surface, and I think as the Test goes on, you know, something will start to happen.“So, we've prepared for all that can come our way, as it is more about the mental challenge in playing these conditions, batting time, bowling those spells and getting the ball in the right areas,” he detailed.India are also deciding on their second seamer alongside Mohammed Siraj. The choice is between Gurnoor Brar and Prasidh Krishna, both of whom have limited Test experience.Morkel said either player would be ready if selected.“I think it's exciting. They've played a lot of cricket back home where it's also tough bowling conditions, and I think coming here the biggest challenge will be the heat and humidity."
Article Summary: Kuldeep Yadav, Ravindra Jadeja and Manav Suthar offer different skills and can form an attacking bowling combination, says bowling coach Morne Morkel. Article Title: India vs Sri Lanka, 1st Test: Galle crosswinds add a layer of intrigue to contest
Article Text:
Indian players during a training session in Galle, Sri Lanka. (ANI Photo)

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

The outcome of the opening Test between India and Sri Lanka, beginning on Saturday in Galle, may be determined not just by the nature of the pitch but by how quickly India’s spinners adapt to the venue’s tricky crosswinds. The picturesque Galle International Stadium, situated beside the Indian Ocean and overlooked by the historic 17th-century Galle fort, has long been a happy hunting ground for spinners.Former India left-arm spinner V Raju believes the winds, particularly the crosswinds, could add a layer of unpredictability to the contest. “Due to the venue’s location, the wind is going to be a factor in the drift the spinners can generate,” Raju told TOI. “There will be crosswinds, so it will depend on how quickly they adjust to it.”Crosswinds can influence the ball’s trajectory, allowing a spinner to purchase greater drift by combining greater revs on the ball to make it float or curve. For batters, that extra fraction of movement could be pivotal in deciding between smothering the drift and getting the outside edge. Nine years ago, R Ashwin and Ravindra Jadeja utilised Galle Stadium’s open setting and robust crosswinds to bamboozle the Sri Lankans with drift and guile.India have arrived on these shores with a wide array of spin options. They have the experience of left-arm spinner Jadeja, who played a crucial role in India’s win in Galle in 2017, the tricks of left-arm wrist spinner bowler Kuldeep Yadav, the precision of left-arm spinner Manav Suthar plus greenhorn off-spinner Saransh Jain.Maninder Singh, another former India left-arm spinner, reckons Suthar could be instrumental to India’s prospects. “He has a rhythmic action with a beautiful seam position. Galle’s crosswinds could be his weapon, provided he learns to use it to his advantage,” Maninder said. The 24-year-old Suthar impressed on debut against Afghanistan, taking 7/62. He followed it up with 11 wickets in two county games for Warwickshire.Maninder also termed Kuldeep a rare talent who deserves a spot in the playing XI regardless of the conditions. “Kuldeep is a bowler who must get more opportunities. I’ve mentioned before that if he had played all the matches during the England tour last year, we would have won the series 3-1,” he said.Yet, the spotlight need not belong to the established names. That’s because at Galle, the best bowler may not be the one who swings the ball the most or turns it square. It may be the one who harnesses the wind the best.
Article Summary: Gale International Stadium has long been a happy hunting ground for spinners. Former India left-arm spinner V Raju believes the winds could add a layer of unpredictability to the contest. R Ashwin and Ravindra Jadeja used the venue’s open setting and robust crosswinds to bamboozle the Sri Lankans with drift and guile.

Article Title: 'Technology saved me': Steve Smith admits he nicked ball despite RTS finding no edge
Article Text:

Australia were bowled out for 198 on the opening day of the first Test against Bangladesh in Darwin, with Steve Smith 's 71 off 109 balls helping them get close to 200 after the rest of the batting order struggled.Smith, however, could have been dismissed for seven if not for a Real Time Snicko (RTS) decision that did not appear to detect an edge.Bangladesh fast bowler Ebadot Hossain made a confident appeal for a catch behind after Smith appeared ready to leave the field. On-field umpire Kumar Dharmasena rejected the appeal before the decision was referred for review.RTS did not show an edge, allowing Smith to continue his innings.Speaking to the media after the day's play, Smith was asked whether he had nicked the ball.“I think so, yeah," said Smith.When asked whether he was fortunate to survive, Smith replied: “I was lucky? Yeah, it seems that way. You got to take it sometimes."Smith was then asked whether the incident had affected his trust in the technology.“Normally it’s pretty good. Maybe I didn’t nick it. I don’t know, but I certainly felt something.If I’d been given out, I was going to walk off. But, yeah, technology saved me today, I guess," Smith said.Smith's innings included seven fours and a six, while Bangladesh pacer Hasan Mahmud took 6/55 from 17 overs.Bangladesh finished the day on 96/1 from 24 overs, reducing their first-innings deficit to 102 runs.Australia opener Jake Weatherald scored 23, the second-highest score in the innings, as the rest of the batting order failed to make a major contribution.

Article Title: 'Udhar nahi jaana': Auqib Nabi recalls how India call-up came as a surprise - Watch
Article Text:
Auqib Nabi

Jammu and Kashmir pacer Auqib Nabi never gave up on his hope of playing Test cricket for India, despite having to wait for his first call-up. He continued to focus on performing, believing that consistent results would eventually earn him a chance.That opportunity came when Nabi was added to India's squad as a replacement for injured fast bowler Jasprit Bumrah for the upcoming two-Test series against Sri Lanka, beginning in Sri Lanka on Saturday.Nabi played a key role in Jammu and Kashmir's first-ever Ranji Trophy title win last season. He said he always believed that his performances would eventually lead to an India call-up."Yes, I had expectations. But the mindset of a cricket player should be of performing and that the other people are watching," Nabi told fellow uncapped player Saransh Jain in a video shared by the BCCI."I knew that I would get the call-up today or tomorrow because when you are doing well for so many years, you are meant to get the returns from the hard work.""So I would bowl with the mindset that my job is to take wickets and perform and the rest is up to the one above. I felt great when my name came up. My family is very happy and I don't think there can be anything greater than this," Nabi added.Saransh, who was part of Madhya Pradesh's Ranji Trophy-winning team in 2021-22 that defeated Mumbai in the final, also spoke about the patience needed to reach the India team.“You have to have patience in Test cricket and if you want to play Test cricket for India, you have to have patience in that too,” the 33-year-old Saransh said.“I made my debut at Ranji Trophy in 2014-15. It's been a long journey. There was a lot of hard work and sacrifices. But I had the belief that one day, I will definitely play for India and for this achievement my family has a big role to play in it.”"My dad, who is a Ranji Trophy player, told me the same thing. You just have to have patience, things will automatically come to you," he added.Both players also recalled how they found out about their India selections."When I got the call, I was driving to the temple. I saw the call and messages in between. That's when I got to know that I was selected,” Saransh said.Nabi said he was at the airport when he received the news.“I was at the airport. We had to go to a camp in CoE and I was about to board a flight to Bangalore."“I got a call asking where I was. I told them that I was going to Bangalore and I was at the airport. They told me that I didn't have to go there; I had to come to Sri Lanka and that I was selected.”“At first, I couldn't believe it. It was unexpected because the squad was already out. I was ready to work hard. I was going to the camp,” Nabi added.
Article Summary: Auqib Nabi was added to India's squad as a replacement for injured Jasprit Bumrah. Nabi played a key role in Jammu and Kashmir's first-ever Ranji Trophy title win last season. He said he always believed that his performances would eventually lead to an India call-up.

Article Title: 'Ball will go soft after 25-30 overs’: Bumrah’s absence adds challenge as Morne Morkel warns India pacers
Article Text:
Galle: From left, India's Mohammed Siraj, Auqib Nabi and Gurnoor Brar during a practice session ahead of the first test cricket match between India and Sri Lanka, in Galle. (PTI Photo)

Morkel urges pacers to adapt quickly

India assess bowling options in warm-up

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

India bowling coach Morne Morkel has highlighted the challenging conditions awaiting the team in Sri Lanka, warning that the combination of heat and humidity could cause the Kookaburra ball to lose its hardness earlier than the Indian seamers are accustomed to. India will begin the first Test against Sri Lanka in Galle on August 15, with their pace attack facing an additional challenge after Jasprit Bumrah was ruled out of the series with a knee injury.With Bumrah unavailable, Mohammed Siraj is now the most experienced seamer in the squad. Prasidh Krishna, Gurnoor Brar and newly called-up Auqib Nabi are the other pace options available to India.Morkel believes India's seamers will need to make the most of the new ball before adjusting their approach once it starts losing its hardness.“Our skill is there, and the planning will be there, but the biggest challenge coming to Sri Lanka is the heat, the humidity, and the Kookaburra ball going soft a little earlier. It will go soft after 25 or 30 overs, so we have to expect that. In these conditions, it’s all about your mindset. If you’re a fast bowler, if you’re going to bowl the shortest spells, the energy you put into the ball and putting it into good areas, you’ll always have opportunity,” Morkel said in pre-match press conference.The former South Africa pacer also stressed the importance of maintaining intensity and building pressure as the Test progresses.“As the Test match will go on, hopefully there will be a little bit of uneven bounce. It’s about how we can stack up overs together with intensity and create that pressure because we haven’t played a lot of red-ball cricket in the last couple of months; going back into that is going to be a challenge as well,” he said.India used the three-day warm-up against the Sri Lanka Cricket XI in Colombo to give their bowling options valuable game time ahead of the Test series.Ravindra Jadeja was among the most effective bowlers, claiming three wickets from 22 overs, while Gurnoor Brar also impressed with three wickets from 20 overs. Kuldeep Yadav and Manav Suthar picked up two wickets each, with the spinners finding considerable assistance during the practice game.Mohammed Siraj bowled 21 overs and took one wicket, while Prasidh Krishna also claimed a wicket from 16 overs. Saransh Jain completed 15 overs without a wicket, while Auqib Nabi bowled five overs as he got a brief opportunity to assess the conditions.
Article Summary: India bowling coach Morne Morkel has highlighted the challenging conditions awaiting the team in Sri Lanka. Morkel warns that the combination of heat and humidity could cause the Kookaburra ball to lose its hardness earlier than the Indian seamers are accustomed to. India will begin the first Test against Sri Lanka in Galle on August 15.

Article Title: Hasan Mahmud's career best 6-55 blows Australia away; Bangladesh take control on day 1 of Darwin Test
Article Text:
Bangladesh's Hasan Mahmud, second left, celebrates with teammates after taking the wicket of Australia's Travis Head during their test match in Darwin, Australia, Thursday, Aug. 13, 2026. (AP)

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Bangladesh's bowlers outperformed Australia's returning Big Four on the opening day of the first Test in Darwin, bowling the hosts out for 198 on Thursday. Hasan Mahmud took a career-best 6-55 as Bangladesh's pace attack kept Australia's batting under pressure. Bangladesh then reached 96-1 by stumps, reducing the first-innings deficit to 102 runs.“Excited to play in Australia,” Hasan said of Bangladesh's first test match in Australia since 2003. “To get the opportunity to play in these conditions as well ... I just tried to maintain the process and just follow what the captain was saying.”Australia won the toss and reached 45 without loss on a green-tinged pitch, but Hasan struck in his sixth and seventh overs to remove openers Jake Weatherald for 23 and Travis Head for 22.Taskin Ahmed took 2-55 and Ebadot Hossain 2-39 as Bangladesh's fast bowlers used a consistent line and length to keep Australia in trouble through the first two sessions.Steve Smith was Australia's main resistance, scoring 71 from 109 balls with seven fours and a six. He was the next-to-last batter dismissed, advancing at Hasan before top-edging a catch to wicketkeeper Litton Das.The day had started with Australia bringing together their first-choice bowling attack.Captain Pat Cummins returned to lead an attack featuring Josh Hazlewood, Mitchell Starc and Nathan Lyon, known as Australia's Big Four.Weatherald, who was playing in front of a home crowd in Darwin, never settled and was caught after swiping at Hasan. Head was then bowled after chopping a delivery from around the wicket onto his stumps.Ebadot dismissed Marnus Labuschagne for one, while Smith was dropped at third slip early in his innings. Bangladesh reduced Australia to 74-4 by lunch after Cameron Green was dismissed for 13.Ebadot removed Alex Carey for 19 after lunch, before Taskin bowled Beau Webster for 12. Hasan then dismissed Cummins for nine and Starc for one before completing his six-wicket haul with the wickets of Smith and Lyon.Australia's bowlers, meanwhile, managed only one Bangladesh wicket before stumps.Shadman Islam made 20 before he edged Starc and was caught by Lyon at cover point, leaving Bangladesh at 36-1.Mominal Haque, on 35, and Tanzid Hasan, on 32, remained unbeaten at the close and shared a 60-run partnership.Smith said Australia's lack of recent Test cricket had contributed to their slow start. The team had not played a Test for eight months.“It can take some time to get into it on occasions,” he said. Batting in the first session “wasn't easy, wasn't a heap of pace on the ball, and it was tacky and seaming around a bit.”The pitch had appeared different to Australia on match day, Smith said.“The bowlers looked at the wicket yesterday and they said it was rock hard, and then today when we rocked up with a bit of dew on the ground, it felt softer,” Smith added. “So hopefully the same tomorrow and the ball starts talking a bit in the morning.”The two-Test series in Australia's Top End is the start of a 12-month schedule that includes 20 Tests for Australia, including tours of South Africa, India and England.
Article Summary: Hasan Mahmud takes a career-best 6-55 as Bangladesh's pace attack keep Australia's batting under pressure. Bangladesh then reached 96-1 by stumps, reducing the first-innings deficit to 102 runs. Steve Smith was Australia's main resistance, scoring 71 from 109 balls with seven fours and a six.

NEW DELHI: Tripura chief minister Manik Saha has fulfilled a promise made to Commonwealth Games gold medallist Asmita Dey, with the state government allotting her a piece of land in Agartala to build a house.The 23-year-old judoka was honoured in Tripura on Wednesday after becoming the first Indian judoka to win a Commonwealth Games gold medal.Dey won the women’s -48kg title in Glasgow after defeating Canada’s Heidi Quach in a dramatic golden-score contest. The state government also presented her with a cheque of Rs 10 lakh as part of the felicitation.Speaking at the event, Saha highlighted Dey’s difficult journey from a small village in South Tripura to the top of the Commonwealth Games podium. Her father was a cycle mechanic at Sonaichari. NEW DELHI: Somewhere on a muddy school field in Haryana right now, a teenager is perhaps drilling the same throwing technique over and over, just as she had watched on television just days ago. Her sole aim is to pull off the one like Sharmila Dhankar, India's Commonwealth Games shot put gold medallist.Before the 2026 CWG campaign, she, like many of us, had almost certainly never heard the name. And it's not because Dhankar had not won anything before the Glasgow Games; she had, a gold medal in the Women's Shot Put F57 event at the 2026 Fazza International Para Athletics Championship, but because one of the primary institutions whose entire job was to carry that story back from the medal podium to villages and training grounds across the state has, for all practical purposes, gone quiet.That's the part of this story that rarely gets told. India walked away from Glasgow with 39 medals, and for a week, the athletes who won them were everywhere, garlanded at airports, seated beside ministers, their faces on the evening news. But medals don't build the next generation of athletes by themselves. Somebody has to keep telling their stories, long after the felicitation photo is filed away, to the kid training in a dusty school ground who needs proof that this path actually leads somewhere.We wanted to know which state sports departments are still doing their job of promoting the sports and their grassroots on their social media platforms, and which ones seem to have simply logged off. So we scrolled through the timelines ourselves. Here's what we found.No state produced more glory in Glasgow than Haryana. Eleven medallists, including seven gold, two silver, two bronze, spanning boxing, wrestling, athletics, and para sport, headlined by a Neeraj Chopra silver that will be replayed on sports channels for years.Alongside him were names most of India still had little knowledge of. The likes of Preeti Pawar, Jaismine Lamboria, Sakshi Chaudhary, Priya Ghanghas, Sachin Siwach, and Ankush Panghal, all of whom trained in government facilities, under government schemes, and who'd probably appreciate their own state department cheering as loudly for them as it does for its concert lineups.Because that's the thing. The Sports Department, Government of Haryana's X account has posted exactly once in all of 2026, and it's a flyer for the music acts playing at the Chief Minister's Cup.Facebook and Instagram follow a similar rhythm with a short cluster of posts around that February event, and then not much else.Eleven medals, and not one dedicated post to show for it. Somewhere in Rohtak or Bhiwani, a young pugilist training in Priya Ghanghas's discipline would probably just like a little proof that someone up top is paying attention.Manipur's page has an odd time-capsule quality to it. This is the state that gave India Mirabai Chanu, one of the country's most beloved Olympic medalists, and this Commonwealth Games alone produced four medalists from Manipur, Chanu's gold among them, alongside Rishikanta Singh, Bindyarani Devi, and Jadumani Singh.And yet the Department of Youth Affairs & Sports' X account hasn't posted since October 2023, a "Run for Unity" event, frozen well before any of this year's medals happened.Although the Facebook page has had a few sporadic posts here and there this year, its Instagram account has managed just two posts since January. It’s the kind of gap that makes you wonder if someone simply forgot the login details somewhere along the way.If there's one number in this whole exercise worth sitting with, it's this: the official Sports Department, Government of Rajasthan hasn't posted on Facebook since April 14, 2012.Fourteen years, through Arundhati Choudhary's Commonwealth gold and everything else that's happened in Rajasthan sport since.Its X account's last original post predates a retweet from March 2021, and there's no Instagram at all. A parallel handle, the Rajasthan State Sports Council, exists across all three platforms and is barely livelier.Somewhere behind Choudhary's medal is a genuinely good story, but it just hasn't found a home on the one page built to tell it.Gulveer Singh managed both a silver and a bronze for Uttar Pradesh this Games, a rare double that would make a great centrepiece for the state's sporting year. Instead, across two separate official handles on three platforms, Uttar Pradesh Sports has produced little beyond reposts, while its sister account, Sports Directorate, Govt of Uttar Pradesh, hasn't posted at all in 2026.Delhi Government, for its part, doesn't run a dedicated sports account at all on any of the popular social media platforms, so gold medalist Harsh Singh and bronze medalist Tejaswin Shankar, both representing India's capital, don't really have an institutional cheerleader online, their wins quietly absorbed into the general churn of city government updates. Both athletes are, in effect, doing their own promotional legwork.Set against all that quiet, Tamil Nadu feels like a different sport altogether. Its Sports Tamil Nadu handles post multiple times a day, celebrating not just its own three medalists, Praveen Chithravel, Selva Prabhu, Muthupandi Raja, but athletes from other states too, weaving in government scheme updates without it ever reading like bureaucracy.Every medallist got a dedicated post. Somewhere in Tamil Nadu, a kid training in long jump or wrestling doesn't have to wonder whether the sport leads anywhere. The state tells them, publicly, almost daily.Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Karnataka's Facebook and Instagram pages, Assam, Bihar, and Tripura all follow a version of that same habit, active, consistent, generous with attention toward athletes nobody outside their district would otherwise know existed.Kerala doesn't run a separate sports handle on X but keeps its Facebook and Instagram genuinely lively, making sure Murali Sreeshankar and Mohammed Basil's silvers got their due.Andhra Pradesh mirrors that same rhythm across all three platforms.Not every state falls neatly into being inactive or staying proactive. Punjab's account managed just two posts on X all year, New Year's and Republic Day, though its Facebook and Instagram carry a bit more life around coaching and departmental meetings, even if athletes rarely get top billing.Uttarakhand was genuinely active last year before cooling off in 2026, leaning more toward government scheme announcements on Facebook, though its Instagram at least carried two posts around the Games.Maharashtra has dedicated posts up for both Sarvesh Kushare and Dilip Gavit, with Instagram staying fairly regular, enough effort to stay out of the quiet column.Karnataka's X account hasn't posted since March 2024, around an unrelated cultural-team event, even though its Facebook and Instagram have stayed warm and active toward its CWG medalists.It is worth asking why this actually matters, beyond good manners. Well, a state sports department's social media feed isn't just a courtesy board for congratulations; it's one of the cheapest, most direct tools available to build the next generation of athletes.A youngster in a small town is far more likely to pick up a javelin because they saw a state government post celebrating someone from their own district. Even when it comes to promoting any government policy, social media can be as effective.Visibility drives aspiration. There's a funding logic too. Sponsors, corporates, and even state finance departments allocate resources partly based on visible public interest, and a well-run social account is often the easiest evidence a sport has that interest.ALSO READ: Anahat Singh: What is in the name? A word from Guru Nanak's prayer, now India's squash sensation Silence, on the other hand, sends the message that grassroots sport isn't a priority worth the effort of a single post, even when the state has just produced a medallist on the world stage.It is worth it because sometimes, the first step towards building a sporting culture is simply showing people that their achievements are being seen.
Article Summary: India won 39 medals at the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow. Haryana produced 11 medallists, including seven gold, two silver, two bronze. But the state sports department has posted just once in all of 2026. What do you think is more important for grassroots sports promotion? Government funding or social media presence? Share your view.

Article Title: ‘That video was not ordinary’: PM Modi praises Lovlina for objecting to distorted India map - Watch
Article Text:
Prime Minister Narendra Modi shares a light moment with boxer Lovlina Borgohain. (PTI Photo)

‘That video was not ordinary’

Mirabai opens up about four difficult years

Narender's joke leaves Modi laughing

NEW DELHI: Boxer Lovlina Borgohain's decision to object to a distorted Indian map during the Commonwealth Games earned special appreciation from Prime Minister Narendra Modi, who described the moment as one that would be remembered for a long time.Lovlina, who won silver in the women's 75kg category in Glasgow, was among India's medal winners who interacted with Modi at his residence on Sunday. The meeting, attended by Sports Minister Mansukh Mandaviya, Minister of State for Sports Raksha Khadse and Indian Olympic Association president PT Usha, saw athletes recount their experiences from the Games in an informal and emotional setting.In a little over 10-minute video of the interaction shared by the Prime Minister's Office on Monday, Modi brought up Lovlina's confrontation with a restaurant in Glasgow after she noticed a distorted Indian map.“Kya hua wo restaurant waale se jhagda kar rahi thi? (What happened, you were fighting with that restaurant guy?)” Modi asked.Lovlina laughed before explaining why she intervened.“We had such a good performance and it was the last day of the Games. It was a happy occasion sir, we were celebrating and I didn't like it when I saw the distorted map. I politely told them and they have made the changes also,” she explained.Modi applauded the boxer for noticing the issue despite being in the middle of celebrations after her medal-winning campaign.“To be able to recognise the significance of that map at a time when you were celebrating and the Games were over, I can tell you truthfully, that video was not ordinary. It will be remembered by people for a very long time,” he told the Tokyo Olympics bronze medallist.India finished fourth in Glasgow with 39 medals, including 13 golds, with boxing contributing seven gold medals.The interaction also provided an emotional window into Mirabai Chanu's journey to her gold medal in the women's 48kg category. The weightlifter produced a Games-record lift of 190kg, but her triumph came after four difficult years following her one-kilogram miss at the Paris Olympics. Modi asked Mirabai about the tears she shed on the podium and even fed her a laddu during their interaction.“Itne aansu tapak rahe the (So many tears were rolling down),” Modi remarked.Mirabai explained that the tears represented years of accumulated emotions.“I was very happy and emotional at that moment. I was crying because I missed a medal in the Paris Olympics by one kilogram. I have faced a lot in these last four years. I was battling injuries and some family problems too.“There were a lot of things. So, these four years were very tough for me. And when I stood on the podium, our flag went up and the anthem played, it was hard to stop myself,” she said.The meeting also had its lighter moments. Boxer Narender Berwal, who won silver in the +90kg category, recalled a funny exchange with a Pakistani boxer after beating him at the 2015 World Military Games.“During the 2015 World Military Games, I had a bout with a Pakistani boxer. I won it but when we were together in the medical room for treatment to our niggles, he said to me 'Bhaijan aapka naam Narender hai, aapke coach ka naam Narender hai, aapke Pradhan Mantri ka naam Narender hai, mujhe Narender naam se nafrat ho gayi hai.' (Brother, you, your coach and your PM are all named Narender. I hate this name now),” he recalled, drawing laughter from Modi.The Prime Minister also underlined the broader significance of the athletes' achievements, saying their medals were helping inspire a new generation.“I have been in this house for 12-13 years now and if there is one group that I have met regularly here, it is the athletes because of your efforts to win medals for India and your tradition of scaling new heights.“Far more than our push to promote sports in schools, it is your medals that inspire people,” Modi said.
Article Summary: Lovlina Borgohain won silver in the women's 75kg category in Glasgow. Prime Minister Narendra Modi described the moment as one that would be remembered for a long time. India finished fourth in Glasgow with 39 medals, including 13 golds, with boxing contributing seven gold medals.

Article Title: ‘From every drop of tears, gold medals are dripping’: PM Modi’s heartfelt message to CWG heroes - Watch
Article Text:
PM Narendra Modi interacted with India's CWG 2026 medal winners at his residence on Sunday. (Pic credit: PM Modi's X post)

Mirabai recalls four years of struggle

‘One family will bring three medals’

India’s Glasgow success

NEW DELHI: “From every drop of tears, gold medals are dripping.”Prime Minister Narendra Modi had an emotional message for Mirabai Chanu as he interacted with India's Commonwealth Games 2026 medal winners at his residence on Sunday, reflecting on the sacrifices behind the country's successful campaign in Glasgow.Modi hosted the medal-winning contingent at 7, Lok Kalyan Marg and heard athletes recount some of the moments that defined their journeys at the Games. India returned from Glasgow with 39 medals, including 13 gold, 17 silver and nine bronze, finishing fourth in the overall standings.During one of the conversations, Modi recalled the emotional scenes surrounding Mirabai's gold-medal triumph.“Tears were falling from you. I feel as if from every drop of tears, gold medals are dripping,” Modi told the Olympic silver medallist.Mirabai, who won gold in Glasgow, opened up about the difficult journey that preceded her Commonwealth Games triumph, including the disappointment of the Paris Olympics.“I was very happy, and emotional too. That day the happiness was greater and I cried because at the Paris Olympics, I lost a medal by 1 kg. In a player’s life what all we have to face. So within these 4 years, how much and what all I had faced, every time injuries were going on and all that was happening.So with great difficulty I had faced these 4 years. So when all that happened, on the podium when I stood, sir, and when our flag goes up and our national anthem plays, sir, we cannot stop, sir, tears come out on their own,” she said.Modi responded by highlighting the wider impact of the athletes' achievements.“This is very good. It is not as if this achievement of yours is considered only your achievement; your victory becomes a very big inspiration for the coming generations.”The informal interaction also saw athletes share lighter and deeply personal moments from their Glasgow campaigns.Modi reminded para shot put gold medallist Sharmila Dhankar of a promise she had made earlier.“You made a promise. Last time, yours, both daughters will become players,” Modi said with a smile.Dhankar replied: “Haanji, right now they are young in age. In the next Commonwealth, one family will bring 3 medals.”Men's 100m T47 gold medallist Dilip Gavit, meanwhile, spoke about dedicating his performance to his guru.“When I was running, when my event was on 29th (July), that day was Guru Purnima, so that day I gave a gift to my guru,” he was heard saying in the video.In another video posted by Modi, gold medallist boxer Sakshi Chaudhary introduced herself and the contingent.“Hello friends! This is Sakshi Chaudhary. Today, our honourable Prime Minister has invited us, the Commonwealth Games medalists, and we feel very proud. We are extremely happy to have met him; he is very humble. Sir, would you like to say something?” she said.Modi replied with a message that summed up his interaction with the athletes: “Jo khelega, woh khilega” (The one who plays, will blossom). “Always cheer for Bharat.”India's fourth-place finish came despite a significantly smaller contingent and a reduced sporting programme compared to Birmingham 2022. India sent 122 athletes to Glasgow, compared to 210 in Birmingham, while 30 of its 61 medals in 2022 came in sports that were not part of the Glasgow programme.Despite those limitations, India retained its fourth-place position and improved its medal conversion rate, with 38 athletes returning home with medals. Long-distance runner Gulveer Singh was the only Indian athlete to win two medals.The Glasgow Games concluded after 11 days, with Scotland handing over the Commonwealth Games flag and ceremonial baton to India ahead of the 2030 edition in Ahmedabad.The symbols were handed to Olympic champion Neeraj Chopra, Indian Olympic Association president PT Usha and Gujarat Deputy Chief Minister Harsh Sanghavi during the closing ceremony.Ahmedabad will become only the second Indian city to host the Commonwealth Games after New Delhi staged the 2010 edition.
Article Summary: PM Narendra Modi hosted medal-winning contingent at 7, Lok Kalyan Marg. Modi heard athletes recount some of the moments that defined their journeys. India returned from Glasgow with 39 medals, including 13 gold, 17 silver and nine bronze.
